subject: Anthropology
title: Totemism
description: A micro-lesson that makes Totemism usable.

hook.text: The eagle clan cannot eat eagles. The bear clan cannot hunt bears. Each group is bound to its animal.

buildup.text: Totemism links human social groups to natural species or objects, creating a sacred bond between society and nature.

discovery.text: Durkheim saw totems as symbols of the group itself. Worshipping the totem meant worshipping society.

twist.text: Lévi-Strauss disagreed. Totems aren't worshipped — they're used to think with, classifying the social world.

climax.text: Totemism shows how humans use nature to organize society — mapping the wild world onto the social one.

punchline.text: Nature provides the symbols; culture gives them meaning.

quiz.question: How did Lévi-Strauss interpret totemism?
options: As a system for classifying the social world

details.summary: Totemism involves a symbolic relationship between a social group and a natural species or object — a clan identified with bear, eagle, or wolf, for example. Lévi-Strauss argued totems are good to think with, providing a natural model for organizing social categories.
details.whyItMatters: Totemism shows how humans use nature to think about society. The relationships between animal species become metaphors for relationships between social groups, revealing the deep human tendency to classify the world symbolically.
takeaways: Totemism links social groups symbolically to natural species
Lévi-Strauss argued totems organize social categories through nature
It reveals how humans use natural distinctions to think about society

faq.question: Does totemism involve worshipping animals?
faq.answer: Not typically. Totemic relationships involve identification, respect, and sometimes dietary restrictions regarding the totem animal. The relationship is symbolic — the bear clan does not worship bears but uses the bear as an identity marker and source of clan cohesion.

faq.question: Is totemism limited to indigenous peoples?
faq.answer: Formal totemism is associated with indigenous societies, but analogous practices appear everywhere. Sports team mascots, national animals, corporate logos, and family crests all use natural or symbolic objects to represent and unify social groups.
